Our new [preprint on protein intake and changes in lean/fat free mass, muscle size, strength, and physical function](https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/view/1166) has prompted the kind of online discussion[^social-media] that almost always follows research on a familiar, practically important topic... particularly one that sits within the weird online world of "science based lifting" where tempers can seemingly flare about the most anodine of things. Some have emphasised our conclusions that the evidence does not identify a clear optimum and that the data are too uncertain to support confident conclusions. Some folks have drawn attention to the small positive trends in the estimates and argued that therefore higher intakes are required for "maximising gains". Those are not merely competing interpretations of our results. I think they illustrate a broader problem in how research travels from a paper, through a post or video, and into advice... particularly when the body of evidence on which that paper is based has a lot of shortcomings and the findings are less certain than many appreciate.

[^social-media]: Admittedly most of this has come to me second hand, as I am no longer on any social media platforms, with the exception of having seen some discussion on reddit and videos on YouTube.

Short-form science communication usually has to leave things out. A social media post can't fully reproduce a methods section, and to be honest it shouldn't have to[^preprint-oa]. The challenge is deciding what can be compressed without misrepresenting the broader message of the work. *“Protein intake showed a modest positive association with outcomes”* is not the same statement as *“more protein produces a meaningful benefit”*; *“We could not identify a clearly optimal intake”* is not evidence that the true curve continues rising indefinitely; even statements like *"higher protein intakes are needed to maximise gains"* aren't strictly speaking accurate despite the aforementioned modest positive associations when what gets left out of the message are things like *“Most trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias"* and *"Publication-bias adjustment attenuated outcome-level estimates towards zero, and certainty was low or very low for all GRADE-assessed contrasts.”* Those distinctions are easy to lose when a complex result is made to fit a caption, thumbnail, or take-home message.

[^preprint-oa]: I mean, part of the reason why for years I have been a big supporter of open access publishing (as well as other open science practices including data, code, and materials sharing), and also the use of preprints, is that the scientific work is openly available to all to read and consider. So folks can see a social media post and then go read the paper themselves if they want to check that the post has done a good job of communicating the findings as they were (which from what I have been told, and seen in some cases, many commentators on posts regarding our new preprint have done themselves).

I don't think this is best understood as a problem of individual commentators behaving badly... the game is the game and it's rigged, so if you don't like it then don't play (like me). The incentives of social media reward clear, confident, emotionally legible conclusions. Scientific evidence is often conditional, uneven, and both frustratingly precise in its detail yet uncertain in its conclusions. It's also long... sooo long, with umpteen supplementary materials[^supplementary] to look through and contextualise the main findings and broader interpretations. 

[^supplementary]: I mean, just take a look at how many bloody supplementary materials we put together for this particular review... we made them their own [website!](https://jamessteeleii.github.io/protein_dose_response_meta/)

That said, there is often a mismatch between the shape of the scientific evidence as it is presented and the shape of the content formats through which many people encounter it. Researchers contribute to that mismatch when we present a review as a verdict, or foreground a neat numerical takeaway while leaving its limitations in the supplement. Personally I try to avoid that as far as possible unless making a particular scientific claim is dictated *a priori* by a defined and pre-registered design and methods for such an inference. Instead I would much prefer to emphasise the uncertainty we still have even if it leaves people having to grapple with the existential dread of not having a single hallowed *number* to pin their flag to.

## What this new review actually leaves us with

The review, linked above, updates and extends earlier syntheses[^everson], bringing together 119 eligible studies identified through out systematic review. Ninety-five contributed sufficient data to the primary analyses: 254 study arms, 4,931 participants, and 1,864 baseline-to-follow-up contrasts. We compared 26 candidate dose-response models across the four outcome groups (whole-body lean/fat-free mass, measures of muscle size or mass, strength, and physical function), including models with no association, linear and spline forms, and smooth nonlinear functions. The purpose was to avoid making the answer depend entirely on choosing one particular function in advance, or even through model comparison methods, instead weighting each model and allowing it to contribute to the overall uncertainty in our estimates. We also examined a huge array of sensitivity and exploratory analyses to consider the variety of assumptions that went into the primary pre-registered analyses and their interpretation, all of which lend caveats to the overall findings.

[^everson]: Specifically the previous review of [Nunes et al. (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8978023/). 

The resulting primary estimates generally show modest positive associations, particularly when protein intake is considered alongside resistance training. But, in my opinion, the central practical question is not whether a fitted average curve slopes up a little. It is whether changing intake by a given amount is likely to produce a change large enough to matter and our level of certainty in that. Under the review’s pre-registered threshold, the evidence did not establish a meaningfully beneficial gain from increasing intake, or a meaningfully harmful loss from decreasing it, across the contrasts we examined. Small changes in intake were generally compatible with practical equivalence, larger differences remained uncertain and we certainly couldn't identify a clear optimal intake.

That is not a finding that protein has no effect, that the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) is optimal for every purpose, or that higher intakes cannot be beneficial for particular people in particular circumstances. Nor does an upward fitted trend from our primary analyses necessarily reflect the magnitude of a causal effect of increasing intake by a specific amount. Sparse data at the low and high ends of the intake range make the shape there especially difficult to establish. Much of the dose-response evidence, given the nature of the arm-based models used, comes from comparisons across intervention arms and studies that differ in more than protein dose in addition to potentially being influenced by post-randomisation variables including things like adherence. The preprint itself is explicit in highlighting that its primary results may overstate the true causal effects of different protein intakes given the stricter within study contrasts, which are closer to the randomised intention to treat estimand, attenuated the dose-response curves magnitude.

But, no matter what fancy analysis we did in order to produce dose-response curves for protein intake, the evidential limitations of the underlying literature matter just as much as the fitted curves. Most included trials raised some concerns or were at high risk of bias; publication-bias adjustment attenuated estimates towards zero; and certainty was rated low or very low according to GRADE for all assessed contrasts. The review is therefore not a high-certainty answer delivered by a sophisticated model. It is a more comprehensive account of a body of research whose limitations still constrain what we can know.

## The evidence pyramid can give the wrong impression

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are often placed at the top of a so called evidence hierarchy[^rothman-dahly], and this one it seems is likely to be treated no differently in the way it is communicated. That placement is sometimes taken to mean that a meta-analysis is inherently more trustworthy than the studies it combines. But synthesis does not repair the issues in the underlying studies. Pooling can reduce random uncertainty when the studies address a sufficiently coherent question. It cannot, by itself, make biased or indirect evidence answer a causal question it was not designed to answer.

[^rothman-dahly]: The original evidence pyramid has, only somewhat tongue in cheek, been supplanted though by the much more nuanced [Rothman-Dahly evidence pyramid](https://zenodo.org/records/18084434) which, to be honest, I am much more inclined to subscribe to

This is why the size, or complexity, of an evidence synthesis should not be confused with the strength of its conclusions. A review can be large, technically demanding, carefully preregistered, fully reproducible and yet still conclude that the evidence is uncertain. Those qualities improve the review. They do not retroactively improve the trials. The strongest contribution of a synthesis may sometimes be to show, in detail, why our confidence should remain limited.

That can be an uncomfortable message in a field accustomed to turning a meta-analysis into a headline: a "breakpoint", a range, or an “optimal” target. A point estimate is easy to repeat. An uncertainty interval and a description of what the evidence cannot distinguish are harder to make memorable. Presenting those in the context of the underlying quality of evidence is even more difficult when space comes at a premium. But when a number, or even a nicely plotted dose-response curve, is presented without the uncertainty and assumptions that produced it, communication has become less accurate even if what's presented has been itself was calculated without error and is technically correct.

## Dose-response modelling is typically exploratory

Sport, exercise, and nutrition science is becoming markedly better at evidence synthesis and we are seeing the application of more sophisticated meta-analytic models in attempts to make the best use of studies that are, individually, often inferentially weak. Dose–response modelling of the kind we've performed in this protein meta-analysis is a good example: rather than asking whether an intervention “works”, we try to estimate how its effects vary across doses. These models can be valuable for decision-making. But fitting the available data is not the end of the scientific job. Despite what Bacon argued, science isn't just induction but, at least under my philosophy, a holistic application of varied logical forms[^book].

[^book]: As I've tried to explain in the [introductory chapter](https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/view/366) for out forthcoming textbook, which should hopefully be published in full by the end of the year! 

A particular dose–response curve may fit the accumulated observations better than its competitors and even cohere with other background knowledge such as mechanistic hypotheses. But, it is still a conjecture[^dose-pred]. If we repeatedly update a flexible model using more studies of the same kind, we risk treating enumerative induction as explanation. Sure, new data might still falsify the implied model, but that's not how it gets used and usually people don't set out to actively try to test it in that manner. But this is the more interesting next step... to ask what the model that we've built predicts about states of the world not used to construct it. If we treat the model as an operationalisation of a theory, it can yield precise quantitative predictions. Those predictions can then inform studies designed as severe tests (i.e., aimed at trying to falsify the theory if it is wrong) rather than as further, weakly powered contributions to a future meta-analysis[^fodder].

[^dose-pred]: That's not to say that dose-response modelling cannot be performed itself as theory testing. But it requires that a theorised dose-response function has been specified a priori to be tested, whether based on prior data or on other theory from which it might be derived. That could be merely conjecturing a particular dose-response shape, or it might be that data or other theory (such as a hierarchical one linking lower level biological mechanisms formally to higher level outcomes) is sufficient to indeed make specific predictions across a range of exposure doses, such that the fit of a pre-specified model to future data can be defined as a test of the model and theory that implies it. But, at present, most dose-response modelling in our field is exploratory, particularly so when done through evidence synthesis methods like meta-analysis.

[^fodder]: Why I tend to view most studies in our field, currently, as at best fodder for this kind of evidence synthesis. I say *currently* because my hope is that this is beginning to change.

## From synthesis to deduction

So, there is still a constructive path forward, but I think it relies on the field grappling with a topic that makes it even more uncomfortable... *epistemology*. As I have tried to explain, dose-response modelling of the kind presented in this new analysis sits very much within an inductive mode of inference. We try to fit models to the data to treat as generalisations. They can help us describe the accumulated evidence and even generate tentative theories that yield predictions about how effects might change with intake which we can take forward and test as hypotheses. A gently rising curve, a saturating curve, or another plausible functional form could each be treated as an exploratory model along with the specific predictions it deductively entails; a conjecture to develop and test severely with new observations rather than treat as some settled biological law. The purpose of model averaging, if it is used as we have, is to represent uncertainty across candidate shapes, not to certify that the averaged curve is the true mechanism.

The next step should be to connect plausible curves to explicit theory, if it exists yet, and derive predictions that could be wrong. If theory predicts a saturating response, perhaps because of the hypothesised involvement of some physiological mechanistic pathway, where should the change become small enough to be practically nothing? Is the theory generalisable in the sense that it's boundary conditions are broad enough to imply similar effects under different training and dietary conditions or different populations? If competing theories imply different responses at low or high intakes, what study could distinguish them? These sorts of questions turn a review from a closing statement into a tool to help guide and plan future research.

But that requires studies to be designed around the uncertainty we have identified, considering the specific nature of the hypotheses the theory implies, and also what auxiliary assumptions are required to test them. For example: larger samples where expected effects are small; adequate representation across the intake ranges about which we want to make claims; more direct and reliable measurement of assigned and achieved intake; transparent reporting of adherence and co-interventions; and outcomes that are important to people and consider both what the theory predicts and also what they would actually consider to be meaningful in terms of their magnitudes. Where feasible, trials that deliberately randomise participants to substantially different protein targets can provide stronger causal information than comparisons that infer a dose-response relationship from a model built across studies. Studies should be powered around testing deductively entailed predictions and meaningful differences intended to either act as falsifiers or corroborators of a theory that implies them, rather than relying on the hope that many small studies will eventually just add up to a decisive answer.

This is the spirit of severe testing: a theory earns support when it survives a test that had a good chance of exposing an important error. A flexible model that accommodates the evidence we already have is useful, but it has not yet passed such a test simply by fitting it to that evidence. We need prospective predictions, informative designs, and results precise enough to discriminate between explanations.

## The point is not to win the protein, or any, debate

The discussion around this preprint can easily become another round in the familiar contest over whether people should eat “more” or “enough” or [insert specific numeric target] protein. That debate may be engaging... for some on social media at least. But it is not the main point I take from the work we've done towards this review. The synthesis shows that a large literature and a sophisticated analysis can still leave substantial uncertainty and highlights the generally low quality of work in the field with respect to answering the questions it apparently cares about. The primary research has not yet provided the information needed for confident, fine-grained recommendations, or even much in the way of broad recommendations.

For people making everyday choices, protein intake is only one consideration among cost, appetite, food preference, health circumstances, energy balance, and training. Our results do not settle every one of those decisions, and they should not be re-purposed as universal dietary advice whether that is to interpret them as "higher protein intakes maximise gains" or "protein doesn't matter". The more important implication for researchers is that claims about precise dose targets have outrun the certainty of the evidence supporting them... and to be honest, it was never that certain in the first place despite the way people presented it[^morton].

[^morton]: For example, the most highly cited meta-analysis of protein dose-response effects is that of [Morton et al. (2018)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28698222/) which continues to be cited more frequently that any of the more recent updates (and if I am being cynical I imagine will probably continue to be despite ours now being the most up to date and comprehensive analysis conducted). Yet, the confidence with which people throw around the "breakpoint" reported in that analysis right from the start outshone the actual confidence in the estimate... even ignoring the other problems with the models used (i.e., not accounting for dependence in effects, not using any weighting in the breakpoint analysis etc.) which would typically lead to narrower and thus overly confident interval estimates, the breakpoint estimates confidence interval still ran from 1.03 to 2.20 g/kg/day which is hardly a certain estimate. 

Social media discussion often treats evidence synthesis, and particularly meta-analysis, as if its job were to settle an argument. I see it differently. In most cases a meta-analysis is a map of the research we have managed to do. In this case, the map shows some broad patterns, large gaps, and a lot of terrain where things are not yet precise enough to guide us confidently. The appropriate response is not to make the map sound more decisive by using a thicker pen to highlight certain parts. It is to improve the research that will let us draw a better one.
